stimulus.title: Natural Science: Why Leaves Turn
stimulus.text:
Every autumn, in the forests of eastern North America and in many other temperate regions, millions of people make trips simply to look at leaves. The spectacle is so familiar that it is easy to forget how strange it is. A maple that was uniformly green in August turns scarlet in October; a birch becomes gold; an oak goes a deep rusty brown. Then, within a few weeks, the leaves fall and the branches stand bare until spring. Some travelers even plan their vacations around predictions of when the color will peak in a particular valley. What is actually happening inside those leaves?

Much of the answer has to do with a pigment called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll is the molecule that allows plants to capture energy from sunlight and use it to make sugars from water and carbon dioxide, the process known as photosynthesis. It absorbs red and blue light strongly but reflects green light, which is why healthy leaves look green to us. During the growing season, a leaf is full of chlorophyll, but the molecule is fragile. Sunlight breaks it down constantly, and the tree must keep producing more to replace it.

As autumn approaches, the days grow shorter and the nights cooler. Trees respond to these signals by preparing for winter, a season in which their broad, thin leaves would be more of a burden than a benefit: they would lose water, be damaged by freezing, and collect heavy snow. One step in this preparation is to stop replacing chlorophyll. Rather than simply abandoning the molecule, the tree breaks much of it down and moves valuable nutrients, especially nitrogen, back into its branches and roots, where they can be stored and reused in spring.

As the chlorophyll disappears, other pigments that were present in the leaf all along become visible. These are the carotenoids, the same family of molecules that make carrots orange and corn yellow. Carotenoids help the leaf capture light and protect it from damage during the summer, but their yellow and orange colors are usually hidden beneath the dominant green. When the green fades, they are revealed. The gold of a birch or a hickory, in other words, is not a new color produced for autumn; it is an old color finally allowed to show.

The brilliant reds and purples of some trees have a different origin. These come from pigments called anthocyanins, which, in many species, are not present in the leaf during the summer at all. Instead, the tree produces them in autumn, at the very time it is shutting the leaf down. This has long puzzled scientists, since making new pigments costs energy that a tree preparing for winter might be expected to save. One leading explanation is that anthocyanins act as a kind of sunscreen, shielding the leaf's remaining machinery from excess light while nutrients are being withdrawn. Other explanations have been proposed, and the question is not fully settled.

Weather influences how vivid the display will be. A run of sunny days and cool, but not freezing, nights tends to produce the most intense reds, because those conditions favor the production of anthocyanins. A warm, cloudy autumn often yields duller colors, and an early hard frost can kill leaves before they reach their peak. Drought during the summer may cause leaves to change color and drop early. This is why the same hillside can look spectacular one year and muted the next.

Finally, at the base of each leaf stem, a layer of specialized cells forms a kind of seam. As the season progresses, this layer weakens until the leaf is held on by little more than a few strands of tissue, and a breeze is enough to carry it away. The scar left on the branch is sealed, protecting the tree through the winter. The leaf, its nutrients already reclaimed, falls to the ground, where it will decay and, in time, return some of what remains to the soil.

One leading explanation is that anthocyanins act as a kind of sunscreen, shielding the leaf's remaining machinery from excess light while nutrients are being withdrawn. Other explanations have been proposed, and the question is not fully settled.

Weather influences how vivid the display will be. A run of sunny days and cool, but not freezing, nights tends to produce the most intense reds, because those conditions favor the production of anthocyanins. A warm, cloudy autumn often yields duller colors, and an early hard frost can kill leaves before they reach their peak. Drought during the summer may cause leaves to change color and drop early. This is why the same hillside can look spectacular one year and muted the next.

Finally, at the base of each leaf stem, a layer of specialized cells forms a kind of seam. As the season progresses, this layer weakens until the leaf is held on by little more than a few strands of tissue, and a breeze is enough to carry it away. The scar left on the branch is sealed, protecting the tree through the winter. The leaf, its nutrients already reclaimed, falls to the ground, where it will decay and, in time, return some of what remains to the soil.

stimulus.title: Natural Science: Why Leaves Turn
stimulus.text:
Every autumn, in the forests of eastern North America and in many other temperate regions, millions of people make trips simply to look at leaves. The spectacle is so familiar that it is easy to forget how strange it is. A maple that was uniformly green in August turns scarlet in October; a birch becomes gold; an oak goes a deep rusty brown. Then, within a few weeks, the leaves fall and the branches stand bare until spring. Some travelers even plan their vacations around predictions of when the color will peak in a particular valley. What is actually happening inside those leaves?

Much of the answer has to do with a pigment called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll is the molecule that allows plants to capture energy from sunlight and use it to make sugars from water and carbon dioxide, the process known as photosynthesis. It absorbs red and blue light strongly but reflects green light, which is why healthy leaves look green to us. During the growing season, a leaf is full of chlorophyll, but the molecule is fragile. Sunlight breaks it down constantly, and the tree must keep producing more to replace it.

As autumn approaches, the days grow shorter and the nights cooler. Trees respond to these signals by preparing for winter, a season in which their broad, thin leaves would be more of a burden than a benefit: they would lose water, be damaged by freezing, and collect heavy snow. One step in this preparation is to stop replacing chlorophyll. Rather than simply abandoning the molecule, the tree breaks much of it down and moves valuable nutrients, especially nitrogen, back into its branches and roots, where they can be stored and reused in spring.

As the chlorophyll disappears, other pigments that were present in the leaf all along become visible. These are the carotenoids, the same family of molecules that make carrots orange and corn yellow. Carotenoids help the leaf capture light and protect it from damage during the summer, but their yellow and orange colors are usually hidden beneath the dominant green. When the green fades, they are revealed. The gold of a birch or a hickory, in other words, is not a new color produced for autumn; it is an old color finally allowed to show.

The brilliant reds and purples of some trees have a different origin. These come from pigments called anthocyanins, which, in many species, are not present in the leaf during the summer at all. Instead, the tree produces them in autumn, at the very time it is shutting the leaf down. One leading explanation is that anthocyanins act as a kind of sunscreen, shielding the leaf's remaining machinery from excess light while nutrients are being withdrawn. Other explanations have been proposed, and the question is not fully settled.

A run of sunny days and cool, but not freezing, nights tends to produce the most intense reds, because those conditions favor the production of anthocyanins. A warm, cloudy autumn often yields duller colors, and an early hard frost can kill leaves before they reach their peak. Drought during the summer may cause leaves to change color and drop early. This is why the same hillside can look spectacular one year and muted the next.

Finally, at the base of each leaf stem, a layer of specialized cells forms a kind of seam. As the season progresses, this layer weakens until the leaf is held on by little more than a few strands of tissue, and a breeze is enough to carry it away. The scar left on the branch is sealed, protecting the tree through the winter. The leaf, its nutrients already reclaimed, falls to the ground, where it will decay and, in time, return some of what remains to the soil.
